kisaltma.Assortativity: Assortativity: the tendency of nodes to tie to similar nodes. A coefficient of +1 means similar nodes choose each other, 0 means choices are random, and negative values mean different nodes choose each other (Newman, 2003).
kisaltma.Homophily: Homophily: the tendency of people with similar attributes (same department, same region) to form ties with each other more often. Measured by the assortativity coefficient and the E-I index.
kisaltma.Louvain: Louvain method (Blondel et al., 2008): splits the nodes into communities in which ties inside a group are as dense as possible compared with ties between groups, by increasing modularity step by step.
kisaltma.PageRank: PageRank (Brin & Page, 1998): measures the importance of a node by the importance of the nodes that tie to it; ties from important nodes raise the score.
kisaltma.ForceAtlas2: ForceAtlas2 (Jacomy et al., 2014): a layout method that pulls tied nodes together and pushes all nodes apart.
kisaltma.LinLog: LinLog energy model (Noack, 2007): a force-directed layout model that clearly separates communities.
kisaltma.QAP: Quadratic Assignment Procedure: tests the association between two network matrices by permuting rows and columns together.
kisaltma.MRQAP: Multiple Regression QAP: explains one network with several network matrices and tests the coefficients by permutation.
kisaltma.E-I: External-Internal index: the difference between ties outside and inside groups divided by all ties.
kisaltma.NMI: Normalized Mutual Information: how far two groupings overlap (0-1).
kisaltma.HITS: Hyperlink-Induced Topic Search: hub and authority scores in a directed network.
kisaltma.GEXF: Graph Exchange XML Format, the network file format of Gephi.

ipucu.veri:
A network consists of nodes (people, organisations, countries, papers) and the ties between them (communication, trade, co-authorship). You can keep several relations among the same nodes, such as an advice network and a friendship network.

Node attributes (department, gender, seniority) are used for colouring, homophily analysis and QAP tests.
ipucu.iliskiler:
Each relation is a separate tie list among the same nodes. The selected relation is analysed in every tab; you can also switch it from the top bar.

You can test how two relations are connected with QAP in the Tests tab.
ipucu.iliski: The relation being analysed. If the project has several relations, switch between them here.
ipucu.agTuru: These two settings affect every measure. The tie list itself does not change; you can switch the setting at any time and compare the results.
ipucu.yonlu:
In a directed network a tie has a source and a target: A may ask B for advice while B does not ask A. In- and out-degree, reciprocity, the triad census and HITS scores are computed only for directed networks.

In an undirected network a tie belongs to both ends (co-authorship, joint membership).
ipucu.agirlikli:
When on, tie values (number of joint papers, trade volume) are used for strength, clustering and the drawing. When off, every tie counts as 1.

Whether weights are used in shortest paths is chosen separately in the Measures tab.
ipucu.dugumler:
Click a cell to edit it directly. Deleting a node also deletes its ties in every relation.

For categorical attributes, values entered earlier are offered as suggestions; use them, because spelling differences count as separate groups.
ipucu.ozellik:
An attribute is a piece of information about each node. A categorical attribute defines groups (department, city); a numeric attribute is measured (age, seniority).

Categorical attributes are used for colouring, the E-I index and the "same group" QAP matrix; numeric attributes for node size and the "difference" QAP matrix.
ipucu.ozTur: An attribute cannot be numeric if one of its values cannot be read as a number. Use a comma or a point for decimals.
ipucu.baglar:
The tie list of the active relation. If there are several rows between the same two nodes, their weights are added in a weighted network and counted as one tie otherwise.

When you add a tie and a name does not exist yet, the node is created automatically.
ipucu.iceAktar:
Paste the data or choose a file; the number of nodes and ties read appears right below. Nodes are matched by name: letter case and extra spaces do not matter.

Adding as a new relation keeps the existing nodes, so you can add a second network (for example friendship) for the same people.
ipucu.iceBicim:
Files read: CSV, TSV, Excel (.xlsx, first sheet), RIS, BibTeX, PubMed (.nbib), Web of Science (.ciw, plain text), EndNote (.enw), Pajek (.net), GEXF, GraphML, UCINET DL.

The separator in CSV files (comma, semicolon, tab) is detected automatically.
ipucu.iceHedef:
New relation: the ties become a separate layer and the existing nodes are kept.

Add to an existing relation: the ties are appended to that list.

Replace the project: everything is deleted and you start over.
ipucu.ikiBicim:
Matrix: rows are actors and columns events; a cell above zero means membership.

Long: one actor and one event on each row. Data from record systems usually come in this form.
ipucu.izdusum: A two-mode network is turned into a one-mode network: two actors who take part in the same event are tied. If you choose the columns, two events that share a member are tied (for example two boards with a common member).
ipucu.izdusumAgirlik:
Count: the number of shared events.

Newman: 1/(k - 1) is added for each event, where k is the number of actors in it. Sharing a crowded event weighs less than sharing a two-person event (Newman, 2001).

Jaccard: shared events divided by the total number of distinct events of the two actors (0-1).
ipucu.enAzYayin: Authors with fewer publications than this are left out. In large bibliographies choosing 2 or 3 makes the drawing simpler.
ipucu.disaAktar: The GEXF file also carries the layout and colours on screen, so Gephi opens with the same view.
ipucu.ayarlar: The number of decimals shown in tables and a note about the project. Calculations always use full precision.
ipucu.agSekme:
The drawing of the network. The settings on the right change the drawing at once; results and measures are not affected.

The drawing is ready for publication: PNG files are saved with 600 dpi resolution information and the SVG file can be edited in drawing software.
ipucu.agEtkilesim: Mouse wheel: zoom. Drag empty space: pan. Drag a node: move it (saved). Click a node: show its details. Hover: highlight its neighbours.
ipucu.yerlesim:
Force: tied nodes attract each other and all nodes repel each other. The LinLog model from the ForceAtlas2 family is used, so communities separate visibly. Four starts are tried and the one with the fewest crossings is kept.

By group: each colour group is laid out on its own and the groups are arranged on a circle.

Circle: nodes are sorted by group and placed on a circle. Rings: nodes highest on the size measure sit in the centre, the lowest on the outside.
ipucu.renk: Nodes are coloured by community, core-periphery, component or an attribute. The 8 largest groups get their own colour and the rest are grey. A numeric attribute is shown in four bands.
ipucu.boyut: A node's area is proportional to the chosen measure (the radius grows with the square root, so the eye is not misled). The legend shows three sample sizes.
ipucu.etiket: Starting from the largest nodes, room is sought for this many labels. A label is placed on one of four sides of its node; if none is free it is hidden. The number of hidden labels is shown in the quality panel.
ipucu.stil: Journal: thin lines and small type, for a paper figure. Slides: thick lines and large type. Poster: soft colours readable from afar. Dark: a dark background.
ipucu.siyahBeyaz: Groups are told apart by shape (circle, square, triangle, diamond, pentagon, hexagon, star, octagon) and grey shades instead of colour. For journals printed in black and white.
ipucu.egri: Curved ties separate straight lines that would overlap and let two reciprocal ties in a directed network appear separately.
ipucu.griBag: When on, only ties inside a group take the group's colour; ties between groups are drawn in grey. This makes the group structure easier to read.
ipucu.ok: The arrowhead showing the target of a tie in a directed network. The arrow ends at the edge of the target node.
ipucu.esik: Ties with a weight below this value are not drawn. This affects only the picture; measures use all the ties.
ipucu.omurga: In very dense weighted networks it keeps the statistically significant ties of each node (disparity filter; Serrano et al., 2009). The smaller α, the fewer ties remain. It affects only the picture.
ipucu.grupAlan: A soft background is drawn around the core members of each group. Distant members that lie outside the group are left out, so the areas do not swell or overlap.
ipucu.grupAd: The group name is written above its area, in a place that does not clash with nodes or other labels.
ipucu.aciklama: The box explaining colours, node size and tie width. When off, the drawing uses the full width.
ipucu.bayrak: If a node name (or the attribute chosen for matching) corresponds to a country, the node is drawn with that country's flag. Countries are recognised by ISO code (TUR, TR) or by their Turkish or English name. If there is a colour group, the ring around the flag takes the group colour.
ipucu.haritaTur:
On world and continent maps the nodes are countries. Regions of a country holds the first-level administrative divisions (provinces, states, regions) of every country; for Türkiye the 81 provinces. Latitude and longitude are read from node attributes for points at any scale, such as cities, districts or facilities. My own map uses any GeoJSON file, such as district or neighbourhood boundaries.

The embedded maps are Natural Earth data (public domain).
ipucu.haritaEslesme: Nodes are placed on the map by this field: the node name or an attribute (for example an ISO code or a province number). Letter case, accents and spaces are ignored. Unmatched nodes are lined up at the bottom left and listed in this panel.
ipucu.agIndir:
PNG single column: 2008 pixels, 600 dpi at 8.5 cm. Double column: 4110 pixels, 600 dpi at 17.4 cm. Slides: 1920 pixels.

SVG: vector, editable in Inkscape or Illustrator. Interactive HTML: a single file with zoom and neighbour highlighting.
ipucu.kalite: Automatic checks on how readable the drawing is: tie crossings, hidden labels, fragmentation, number of groups and density. The suggestions do not change the drawing; they only give guidance.
ipucu.olcuSekme: Network-level measures describe the whole network and node-level measures the position of each node. Click a heading to sort the table.
ipucu.agDuzeyi: The size, density, fragmentation, distances, clustering and centralisation of the network. The "?" next to each measure explains what it means.
ipucu.yolAgirlik:
When on, shortest paths use tie weights: a strong tie counts as a short path (distance = 1 / weight; Newman, 2001). Betweenness and closeness change accordingly.

When off, every tie is one step. If the weight is a cost or a distance (km, time) keep this off.
ipucu.dugumDuzeyi: The centrality and structural measures of each node. The bar in the sorted column shows the value relative to the highest one. You can download the whole table as CSV or Excel.
ipucu.dereceDagilim: The complementary cumulative distribution: for each k, the share of nodes with at least k ties. A straight line on a log-log scale points to a heavy-tailed distribution in which few nodes collect many ties.
ipucu.dagilim: Two chosen measures plotted together. For example, nodes with low degree but high betweenness are brokers that link different groups with few ties.
ipucu.merkezKorelasyon: How far the measures put the nodes in the same order (Spearman ρ). A value near 1 means the two measures tell the same story; a low value means they capture different kinds of centrality.
ipucu.grupSekme: Communities are found from the tie structure alone; attributes are not used. The homophily section tests how ties are distributed by an attribute (department, gender).
ipucu.louvain: The Louvain method (Blondel et al., 2008) moves nodes step by step to the communities that raise modularity most, then merges communities and starts again. Because the result depends on the random start, it is run many times and the partition with the highest Q is kept.
ipucu.cozunurluk: γ = 1 is standard modularity. Larger γ finds more and smaller communities; smaller γ finds fewer and larger ones (Reichardt & Bornholdt, 2006).
ipucu.tekrar: How many different random starts Louvain is run with. Stability is calculated from these runs. 30 is enough for most networks.
ipucu.modulerlik: How many more ties fall inside communities than expected in a random network with the same degrees (Newman & Girvan, 2004). Roughly 0.3 and above is taken as a clear community structure.
ipucu.qAralik: The lowest and highest modularity across all runs. A narrow range means the result does not depend on the start.
ipucu.kararlilik: How far a node's community in the best partition overlaps with its community in each run (mean of Jaccard similarities, 0-1). A value near 1 means the node always stays in the same community.
ipucu.renkDuzen:
You can give your own colours to the eight largest groups of the attribute chosen for colouring (for example continent or community). Click the colour box and choose a colour; choices are kept separately for each colouring criterion. If there are more than eight groups, the rest are drawn grey as “Other”.

If colouring is set to “No colour”, you can choose the colour of all nodes from a single box. The colour choice is hidden while black-and-white print is on.
ipucu.imzaYazi:
A small “Ağ Masası (Çetin, 2026)” mark is added to the lower right corner of the figure, so that the tool used remains visible wherever the figure is reused.

Some journals do not accept software names inside figures; in that case you can turn the mark off. When you do, a note appears from which you can copy the source line for under the figure and the reference entry.
ipucu.sekilKaynak:
Journals print a source line under each figure. When you publish a figure made with Ağ Masası, we kindly ask you to add this line under the figure and to list the tool in your references. Citation formats are in the “How to cite” window in the File menu.

In English the name is also given as “Ag Masasi”, so that readers who cannot type Turkish letters can find the tool.
ipucu.veriKaynagi: If you use this sample data in your own work, we kindly ask that you cite both the NGO Shipbreaking Platform, the source of the data, and Filiz and Çetin (2026), the study on which the design of the network is based.
ipucu.makaleKiyas: The table shows the values published in the article next to those computed from this network. Small differences can occur because the Platform corrects its lists as new information arrives. For 2014 and 2017 the node, tie and degree values agree with the article.
ipucu.toplulukAdi: Click a community name to change it; the new name is used in the drawing, the legend and the reports. The name is tied to the members: when the method runs again, a community whose members stay largely the same keeps its name.
ipucu.icYogunluk: The share of possible ties inside the community that are present.
ipucu.nmi: Normalised mutual information (Danon et al., 2005): how far the communities match the groups of an attribute. 1 is a perfect match and 0 no relation.
ipucu.toplulukOzellik: The communities found are saved as a node attribute called "Community", so you can use them in a QAP test or in exported files.
ipucu.matrisGorunum: The adjacency matrix sorted by community. Dark squares on the diagonal show dense ties inside communities; dots off the diagonal show ties between communities.
ipucu.benzesme: The tendency of similar nodes to form ties (homophily). The E-I index compares ties inside and outside groups, and the assortativity coefficient answers the same question as a correlation.
ipucu.ei:
E-I = (external - internal) / (external + internal) (Krackhardt & Stern, 1988). -1 means all ties are inside groups and +1 that all are outside.

Because of group sizes the value may not be 0 even at random, so it is read together with the value expected at random.
ipucu.eiP: The attribute values are shuffled among the nodes thousands of times and E-I is calculated each time. p is how often a value as extreme as the observed one appears among the shuffles. Below 0.05 is usually taken as significant.
ipucu.uyumKat: Categorical assortativity (Newman, 2003): 1 means ties fall entirely within the same group, 0 random, and negative values that they concentrate between different groups.
ipucu.uyumSayi: The correlation of the values at the two ends of each tie: a positive value means nodes with similar values (for example people of similar age) are tied.
ipucu.yapiSekme: Analyses of the inner arrangement of the network. The small-world and robustness calculations take time in large networks, so they start with a button.
ipucu.cekirdekCevre: The discrete model of Borgatti and Everett (2000) splits the network into a densely tied core and a periphery that is loosely tied to the core and sparse within itself. The split is found by local search so as to maximise the correlation between the observed network and the ideal pattern.
ipucu.cpUyum: The Pearson correlation between the observed ties and the ideal core-periphery pattern. 0.5 and above points to a strong core-periphery structure.
ipucu.blokYogunluk: The share of possible ties present in the core-core, core-periphery and periphery-periphery blocks. Ideally the first is high and the last close to zero.
ipucu.cpYoksay: When on, ties between core and periphery do not count in the fit (the recommended model). When off, those ties are expected to be present too.
ipucu.aracilar: Nodes that link different groups. Betweenness measures how many shortest paths pass through a node, and constraint (Burt, 1992) how far its neighbours are tied to each other. Nodes with high betweenness and low constraint fill "structural holes".
ipucu.kesmeNoktasi: A node whose removal splits the network (or its component) into several parts. A bridge is a tie that does the same. Found with the method of Hopcroft and Tarjan (1973).
ipucu.kCekirdek: A k-core is the largest subnetwork in which every member has at least k neighbours inside it (Batagelj & Zaveršnik, 2003). The highest core is the most tightly knit centre of the network.
ipucu.kucukDunya: σ = (C / Cr) / (L / Lr) (Humphries & Gurney, 2008). C is clustering and L mean distance; r denotes networks rewired at random while keeping the degrees (Maslov & Sneppen, 2002). σ > 1 means a small world.
ipucu.sigma: Above 1 means the network is much more clustered than its random equivalents but has paths almost as short. It is computed on the largest component.
ipucu.triad: In a directed network every group of three nodes falls into one of 16 types by the pattern of ties among them (Batagelj & Mrvar, 2001). For example 030T shows a transitive hierarchy, 030C a cycle and 300 a fully mutual triple.
ipucu.diad: Each pair of nodes is mutual, asymmetric or null. Reciprocity shows how many of the tied pairs are mutual.
ipucu.dayaniklilik: Nodes are removed one by one and the share left in the largest part is tracked at each step. In a targeted attack the best-connected or strongest broker nodes go first (degree is recalculated at each step); the random scenario averages 20 different orders.
ipucu.rEndeks: R is the area under the curve divided by the number of nodes (Schneider et al., 2011). A value near 0.5 shows a robust network and a value near 0 a fragile one.
ipucu.testSekme:
There are five tests. QAP and MRQAP compare relations with each other or with node similarity. Comparison with random networks tests whether network-level measures could be due to chance. Attribute and position checks whether the centrality of nodes depends on an attribute. Assortativity measures whether similar nodes choose each other. Significance of community structure compares the communities found with random networks.

Since observations in network data are not independent, all of them derive the p value from permutations or random networks. The formula of each test is shown in the box on the right.
ipucu.bagimli: The relation to be explained, for example co-authorship. Each cell of the matrix is a pair of nodes.
ipucu.bagimsiz: Another relation or a matrix derived from an attribute. For a categorical attribute the cell is 1 if both nodes are in the same group and 0 otherwise. For a numeric attribute the cell is the absolute difference between the two values.
ipucu.permSay: More shuffles give a more stable p value but take longer. At least 1000 is recommended for reported results.
ipucu.qap: The rows and columns of the dependent matrix are shuffled together in the same order and the correlation is recalculated each time (Krackhardt, 1988). p (≥) is how often a correlation as large as the observed one appears, p (≤) how often one as small appears.
ipucu.mrqap: A permutation version of multiple regression for network data. In double semi-partialling (Dekker et al., 2007) the residuals of each predictor, cleaned of the other predictors, are shuffled; this gives reliable p values even when the predictors are correlated.
ipucu.betaStd: The standardised coefficient, for comparing the effects of predictors on different scales.
ipucu.raporSekme: The method text describes only the analyses that were actually run and cites the source of each method. Edit it to fit your own study.
ipucu.yontemMetni: A draft for the method section of a paper or thesis. The references are in APA 7 style and were checked against Crossref records.
ipucu.rapor:
Word report: the network drawing, network-level measures, the most central nodes, communities, homophily, core-periphery, brokers and, if run, the tests; then the method text and references.

Excel: all the measures of every node, the network-level measures, the tie list, communities and QAP results.
ipucu.yardimSekme: Pick a topic on the left or search. Click a figure to enlarge it.
ipucu.o_derece: The number of ties a node has (Freeman, 1978). The simplest and often the most telling centrality measure: how many others a node is directly connected to.
ipucu.o_dereceGiris: The number of ties coming into a node: how many chose it or asked it for advice. An indicator of popularity or prestige.
ipucu.o_dereceCikis: The number of ties going out of a node: how many it chose. An indicator of activity or outreach.
ipucu.o_guc: The sum of tie weights. For example the total number of an author's joint papers.
ipucu.o_gucGiris: The sum of the weights of incoming ties.
ipucu.o_gucCikis: The sum of the weights of outgoing ties.
ipucu.o_arasindalik: The share of shortest paths between other pairs of nodes that pass through this node (Freeman, 1978; Brandes, 2001). Normalised to the range 0-1. A high value marks a broker that can control the flow of information.
ipucu.o_yakinlik: The inverse of a node's mean distance to the nodes it can reach, corrected by the share of reachable nodes in disconnected networks (Wasserman & Faust, 1994). A high value marks a node that can reach everyone quickly. In directed networks outgoing paths are used.
ipucu.o_harmonik: The mean of the inverse distances (Marchiori & Latora, 2000). An unreachable node contributes 0, so it is more reliable than closeness in fragmented networks.
ipucu.o_ozvektor: Centrality proportional to the centrality of the nodes one is tied to (Bonacich, 1972): being tied to important people matters. Scaled so that the highest value is 1.
ipucu.o_pagerank: The probability that a walker following ties at random is at this node (Page et al., 1999; damping 0.85). In directed networks it rewards the quality of incoming ties.
ipucu.o_hub: In the HITS method (Kleinberg, 1999) a node that points to good authorities gets a high hub score.
ipucu.o_otorite: In the HITS method a node that is pointed to by good hubs gets a high authority score.
ipucu.o_cekirdek: The highest k-core a node belongs to (Batagelj & Zaveršnik, 2003). A high number means belonging to the tightly knit centre.
ipucu.o_kumelenme: The share of a node's neighbours that are tied to each other (Watts & Strogatz, 1998). A high value means being in a tight circle where everyone knows each other.
ipucu.o_kisitlama: Burt's (1992) constraint: how far a node's ties are concentrated on neighbours who are also tied to each other. A low value marks a node that joins groups who do not know each other and fills structural holes.
ipucu.o_etkinBuyukluk: Burt's (1992) effective size: the number of neighbours minus the redundancy from ties among them. Neighbours who are disconnected from each other give a high value.
ipucu.a_n: The number of nodes in the network, including those without ties.
ipucu.a_m: The number of ties. Repeats between the same pair count as one tie.
ipucu.a_yogunluk: The share of possible ties that are present (0-1). Density naturally falls in large networks; when comparing networks of different sizes also look at the mean degree.
ipucu.a_ortDerece: The average number of ties per node. In a directed network the mean in- and out-degree are equal and give this value.
ipucu.a_bilesenSay: The number of parts that cannot reach each other by any path. Every node without ties is a separate component.
ipucu.a_enBuyukOran: The share of nodes in the largest component. Distance measures and the small-world test mainly describe this part.
ipucu.a_ortUzaklik: The mean shortest-path length over all pairs of nodes that can reach each other.
ipucu.a_cap: The shortest path between the two farthest nodes that can reach each other.
ipucu.a_gecislilik: The share of closed triples among all connected triples: how far "a friend of my friend is my friend" holds.
ipucu.a_ortKumelenme: The mean of the nodes' local clustering coefficients (Watts & Strogatz, 1998). It can differ from transitivity because it gives equal weight to poorly connected nodes.
ipucu.a_karsiliklilik: How many of the tied pairs are tied both ways. Meaningful only in directed networks.
ipucu.a_dereceUyumu: The correlation of the degrees at the two ends of each tie (Newman, 2002). A positive value means well-connected nodes are tied to each other, a negative value that they are tied to poorly connected ones.
ipucu.a_merkDerece: Freeman (1978) centralisation: how much the network resembles a star centred on a single node (0-1).
ipucu.a_merkArasindalik: How far betweenness is concentrated in a single node (0-1). A high value shows that the flow depends on one broker.
ipucu.nullModel:
Same number of nodes and ties: ties are placed at random between nodes; only density is kept. This is the conditional uniform graph (CUG) test (Anderson et al., 1999).

Same degree sequence: the ends of two ties are swapped many times, so every node keeps its degree (Maslov & Sneppen, 2002). This shows whether a result comes only from a few highly connected nodes. Degree centralisation does not change under this model, so it is left out of the table.
ipucu.dugumY: A measure of the node's position in the network, or a numeric attribute. For example in-degree, betweenness or PageRank.
ipucu.dugumX: With a categorical attribute the difference between groups is measured by the F statistic; with a numeric attribute the association is measured by Pearson correlation. The p value is found by shuffling the attribute values among the nodes, so the dependence in network data does not mislead the result (Borgatti et al., 2018).
ipucu.asortX: For categorical attributes Newman's assortativity coefficient is computed; for numeric attributes, the correlation between the values at the two ends of a tie (Newman, 2003). Values near +1 mean similar nodes choose each other, 0 means chance, and negative values mean different nodes choose each other.

agAnalizi.m:
Most analyses look at people, organisations or countries one by one: their income, their staff, their exports. Network analysis looks at the relations between them instead: who gets advice from whom, which country sells to which, which authors write together.

Some things only become visible when the relations are seen as a whole: a broker everyone passes through, groups closed in on themselves, or a node whose removal breaks the structure apart. Network analysis studies not the parts but the structure they form together.

A network has two basic elements. Nodes are the units studied: people, organisations, countries, papers. Ties are the relations between them: advice, trade, co-authorship, citation. From these two lists Ağ Masası computes who is central, which groups form and how robust the structure is.

Example questions:

  • In a department, through whom does information flow, and who is left alone?
  • Which countries does international or interregional trade depend on, and how much weaker does the network get if one is removed?
  • Do researchers in a field form groups cut off from each other?
  • Do people in the same unit collaborate with each other more?

Network analysis is used in economics, management, international relations, sociology, political science, education, health, logistics and science mapping, among other fields (Wasserman & Faust, 1994).

nedir.m:
Ağ Masası is a free browser-based tool for social network analysis. It draws the relations between people, organisations, countries or publications as a network, measures the structural properties of the network and of each node, tests the results statistically and gives you everything as a report.

The tool is a single HTML file. It needs no installation, account or internet connection, and your data never leave your computer. The project is saved in the browser automatically, but you should download the project file regularly as a backup.

The calculations were verified against the widely used NetworkX and igraph libraries.

ilkAdim.m:
1. Data: In the Data tab choose "Edge list" and paste two or three columns (source, target, weight) from Excel. Tick the box if the network is directed.
  2. Attributes: If you have them, add department, gender and so on with "Node attributes".
  3. Network: In the Network tab link colour to an attribute or to communities and size to a centrality measure.
  4. Measures: Read the density of the network and the most central nodes.
  5. Groups and Structure: Look at communities, homophily, core-periphery and brokers.
  6. Report: Download the Word report and edit the method text to fit your study.

Opening the sample project and going through the tabs is the quickest way to see what the tool produces.

veriHazirlama.m:
Network data usually come from surveys ("whom do you turn to most for advice at work?"), records (email, co-authorship, trade) or documents. Before the analysis decide on:

  • Boundary: Who is in the network? People who did not answer the survey leave gaps; mention this in the report.
  • Direction: Does the tie go from one side to the other (advice) or is it shared (co-authorship)?
  • Weight: Does a number show the strength of the tie (frequency, volume)?
  • Names: The same person must be written the same way everywhere. The tool ignores letter case and extra spaces, but "A. Kaya" and "Ali Kaya" become two nodes.

Using codes (P01, P02) instead of names protects privacy for personal data; you can keep the names in a separate table.

bicimler.m:
Edge list: one tie per row. The first two columns are node names, the third an optional weight.

Adjacency matrix: a square table; row i, column j is the value of the tie from i to j. If the matrix is not symmetric the network is taken as directed.

Two-mode data: two kinds of nodes such as person-event or firm-project, projected to a one-mode network.

Bibliography: a co-authorship network from an RIS, BibTeX, PubMed, Web of Science or EndNote export.

Other programs: Pajek .net, Gephi .gexf, GraphML and UCINET DL files; direction and attributes are read from the file.

In Excel files the first sheet is read. In CSV files the separator is detected automatically.

iliskilerY.m:
The same people can have different kinds of ties: advice, friendship, joint projects. Ağ Masası keeps them as separate relations on the same nodes. The node list and the attributes are shared.

The analysis always runs on the selected relation; switch between relations with the selector in the top bar. In the Tests tab you can test with QAP whether one relation explains another, for example "does working on the same project explain co-authorship?"

yonluAg.m:
In a directed network a tie from A to B can exist without one from B to A. In-degree (how many chose this person) and out-degree (how many this person chose) then mean different things, and reciprocity, the triad census and HITS scores are computed. Closeness uses outgoing paths; clustering and communities ignore direction.

In a weighted network a tie has a value. Strength (weighted degree), modularity, E-I, QAP and the line width in the drawing use the weight. Using weights in shortest paths is a separate choice: turn it on if the weight is a closeness (frequency) and keep it off if it is a cost (km).

ozelliklerY.m:
Attributes are information about the nodes. There are two kinds:

  • Categorical: department, gender, city. Used for colouring, group areas, the E-I index, categorical assortativity and the "same group" matrix in QAP.
  • Numeric: age, seniority, income. Used for node size, numeric assortativity and the "difference" matrix in QAP.

You can import attributes as a table or edit them one by one in the table on the Data tab. You can also save the communities found in the Groups tab as an attribute.

ikiModY.m:
In a two-mode network ties exist only between two different kinds of nodes: people and the events they attend, directors and the boards they sit on. Since most network measures are defined for one-mode networks, the data are projected onto one kind: two people who attend the same event are tied.

The tie weight can be computed in three ways. Count is the number of shared events. With the Newman weight each event contributes 1/(k - 1), so sitting together in a 50-person meeting weighs less than a two-person piece of work (Newman, 2001). Jaccard is the number of shared events divided by the total number of distinct events of the two people.

kaynakcaY.m:
Choose the bibliography file you exported from Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed or Zotero. Every pair of authors on the same publication is tied; the tie weight is the number of joint papers, or the Newman weight reduces the effect of long author lists.

Authors are matched by surname and first initial ("Kaya, A."). This removes most spelling differences between databases, but it can merge two different people with the same surname and initial. Check such cases in the node table on the Data tab.

Each author's number of publications is added as the "Publications" attribute, which you can use for node size.

yerlesimY.m:
In a force-directed layout tied nodes pull each other like springs and all nodes push each other apart like charged particles. Ağ Masası uses the LinLog model from the ForceAtlas2 family (Jacomy et al., 2014; Noack, 2007). This model separates communities clearly, so clusters that sit close together in the figure really are densely tied.

The layout starts from a random position. Four starts are tried and the one with the fewest tie crossings is kept; then overlapping nodes are pushed apart and the figure is rotated so its widest direction is horizontal. "Lay out again" tries a new start. The same network and seed always give the same result.

In networks larger than 300 nodes the repulsion is computed with the Barnes-Hut approximation, so networks of a few thousand nodes are laid out in seconds.

haritaY.b: Networks on a map and flags
haritaY.m:
In trade, migration, transport or collaboration networks the geographic position of nodes is part of the meaning. When On a map is chosen as the layout in the Network tab, nodes are placed at their locations and ties are drawn over the map.

  • World and continents: nodes are countries, recognised by ISO code (TUR, TR) or by Turkish or English name ("ABD", "USA", "Türkiye", "Turkey" count as the same country).
  • Regions of a country: the provinces, states or regions of every country are embedded. In Türkiye provinces match by name or plate number (06, 6, TR-06).
  • Latitude and longitude: for points at any scale such as cities, districts, ports or factories, two numeric attributes are chosen; country borders are drawn in the background.
  • My own map: any GeoJSON file with district, neighbourhood or statistical region boundaries can be loaded; the field holding the region name is found automatically.

If the nodes are countries they can be shown with flags; the colour group shows in the ring around the flag. Maps come from Natural Earth (public domain) and flags from flag-icons (MIT licence); both are embedded, so no internet connection is needed.

renkBoyut.m:
Colour shows a group: community, core-periphery, component or a categorical attribute. The eight largest groups get their own colours; the palette (Okabe-Ito) stays distinguishable for colour-blind readers. If a numeric attribute is chosen, its values are split into four bands.

Size shows a measure. A node's area is proportional to its value; because the radius grows with the square root, a node with twice the value looks twice as large, not four times.

Group areas draw a soft background around the core members of each group (those with at least half of their neighbours in their own group). Distant members are left out, so areas do not overlap and do not hide the real structure of the network.

etiketY.m:
Overlapping labels are the biggest reason network figures become unreadable. Ağ Masası places labels starting from the largest node: for each label it tries the right, left, top and bottom of the node; the label is written if it does not clash with another label or node and hidden if no place fits.

The number of hidden labels appears in the quality panel. On screen the name appears when you hover over a node, and the label of the node you select is always written. Labels have a white halo so they stay readable over ties.

For journal figures 10-20 labels are usually enough; the other nodes can be given in a table.

stillerY.m:
The same network can be drawn in four styles. Journal uses thin lines and small type. Slides thickens the lines and enlarges the type. Poster uses soft tones. Dark is a dark background for screen presentations.

When black-and-white print is on, groups are told apart by shape (circle, square, triangle, diamond, pentagon, hexagon, star, octagon) and grey tones instead of colour. The legend shows the same shapes.

omurgaY.m:
When very dense networks are drawn, everything seems tied to everything. There are two remedies. Minimum weight hides ties below a value; it is simple but can leave weakly tied nodes completely isolated.

The backbone (disparity filter; Serrano et al., 2009) decides separately for each node: a tie is kept if it takes a clearly larger share of that node's total tie weight than expected at random. This keeps the important ties of both strong and weak nodes. The smaller α, the stricter the filter.

Both settings affect only the drawing; measures are computed with all the ties. The report states when the backbone was used.

disaAktarY.m:
PNG files are saved with 600 dpi resolution information: single column for an 8.5 cm width, double column for 17.4 cm. These sizes meet the figure rules of most journals.

SVG is a vector file; open it in Inkscape, Illustrator or Affinity to edit text and colours. Interactive HTML is a single file with zoom and neighbour highlighting that can be emailed or put on a web page.

The export on the Data tab gives the network for Gephi (GEXF, with on-screen positions and colours), Cytoscape and igraph (GraphML), Pajek (.net) and UCINET (DL).

derece.m:
Degree is the number of direct ties a node has (Freeman, 1978). It shows how many others a person is in direct contact with and is often the most telling centrality measure. In a directed network in-degree shows popularity or prestige and out-degree activity.

Strength is the weighted degree: the sum of tie weights. Two authors may have the same degree while one wrote a single paper with each co-author and the other ten.

The degree distribution shows how tie counts are spread across nodes. A straight line on a log-log scale points to a heavy-tailed distribution in which a few hubs collect most ties.
derece.sa: Degree in the kite network: D has the most ties.

arasindalik.m:
Betweenness measures how many of the shortest paths between other pairs of nodes pass through a node (Freeman, 1978). A node with high betweenness is a broker that can control the flow of information or resources between groups. If it leaves, many paths lengthen or break.

It is computed with the Brandes (2001) algorithm and normalised to 0-1: the value is divided by the highest possible betweenness (the centre of a star). If weighted paths are on, strong ties count as short paths.

Betweenness can be high even for nodes with low degree. In the kite network H has only three ties, but every path to the two nodes on the right passes through it.
arasindalik.sa: Betweenness in the kite network: H is highest.

yakinlikY.m:
Closeness is the inverse of a node's mean distance to the other nodes. A high value marks a node that reaches everyone in few steps, from which information is thought to spread quickly. If the network is fragmented, the Wasserman and Faust (1994) correction is applied: the value is multiplied by the share of reachable nodes.

Harmonic closeness (Marchiori & Latora, 2000) is the mean of the inverse distances. An unreachable node contributes zero, so it is more consistent in fragmented networks.

In a directed network closeness uses outgoing paths: how quickly can this node reach others?
yakinlikY.sa: Closeness in the kite network: F and G are closest.

ozvektorY.m:
These measures rest on the idea that "being tied to important people makes you important". Eigenvector centrality (Bonacich, 1972) keeps a node's score proportional to its neighbours' scores, scaled so the highest is 1.

PageRank (Page et al., 1999) is the probability that a walker who follows ties at random, and now and then jumps to a random node, is at this node. In directed networks it rewards both the number and the quality of incoming ties.

HITS (Kleinberg, 1999) separates two roles in a directed network: hubs that point to good authorities and authorities that are pointed to by good hubs.
ozvektorY.sa: Eigenvector in the kite network: D is highest.

yerelYapi.m:
Local clustering is the share of a node's neighbours who are tied to each other (Watts & Strogatz, 1998). A high value marks a tight circle where everyone knows everyone; such circles have high trust and solidarity but little new information.

Burt (1992) calls the opposite a structural hole: a node that bridges people who do not know each other gains access to information from different circles. Constraint is how far a node's ties are concentrated on neighbours who are also tied to each other; low constraint means a structural-hole opportunity. Effective size is the number of neighbours minus the redundancy among them.
yerelYapi.sa: Constraint in the kite network: the circled node is the most constrained.

agOlcuY.m:
• Density: the share of possible ties that are present. It falls naturally in large networks; also look at the mean degree when comparing.
  • Components: parts that cannot reach each other by any path. The share of the largest component shows how integrated the network is.
  • Mean distance and diameter: the typical and the longest number of steps between two nodes.
  • Transitivity and mean clustering: how far "a friend of my friend is my friend" holds. The first counts all triples, the second gives each node equal weight.
  • Reciprocity: in a directed network, the share of ties that go both ways.
  • Degree assortativity: whether well-connected nodes tie to each other (positive) or to poorly connected ones (negative) (Newman, 2002).
  • Centralisation: how much the network resembles a star around a single centre (Freeman, 1978).

louvain.m:
A community is a cluster of nodes densely tied within and sparsely tied outside. Ağ Masası finds communities with the Louvain method (Blondel et al., 2008): each node moves to the neighbouring community that raises modularity most; when nothing changes, communities are merged into single nodes and the process repeats.

Modularity (Q) is how many more ties fall inside communities than expected in a random network with the same degrees (Newman & Girvan, 2004). Roughly above 0.3 counts as a clear structure.

Louvain's result depends on the starting order, so the method is run many times (30 by default) in different random orders and the partition with the highest Q is used. The resolution (γ) lets you look for smaller or larger communities (Reichardt & Bornholdt, 2006).

kararlilikY.m:
One Louvain run may put some nodes in one community and the next run in another. Ağ Masası measures this instead of hiding it: a node's stability is the mean Jaccard similarity between its community in the best partition and its community in each run. A value near 1 means the node always stays put; a low value means it sits on a border.

NMI (normalised mutual information; Danon et al., 2005) is the overlap between the communities found and the groups of an attribute. For example, if communities match departments with NMI = 0.8, collaboration mostly stays within department lines.

benzesmeY.b: Homophily: the E-I index and assortativity
benzesmeY.m:
People tend to form ties with those who resemble them (homophily). The E-I index (Krackhardt & Stern, 1988) compares external (E) and internal (I) ties: (E - I) / (E + I). -1 means all ties are inside groups and +1 that all are outside.

If group sizes are unequal, E-I is not zero even in a random network. So Ağ Masası shuffles the attribute values thousands of times to compute the expected value and how unusual the observed value is (p).

Assortativity (Newman, 2003) answers the same question as a correlation; for numeric attributes (age, seniority) it is the correlation of the values at the two ends of each tie.

matrisGorunum.m:
The adjacency matrix shows the network as a table: a filled cell means a tie. When rows and columns are sorted by community, communities appear as dark squares on the diagonal; dots off the diagonal are ties between communities.

In dense networks the matrix view is easier to read than a node-link drawing because lines do not overlap. It is shown for networks of up to 400 nodes.

cekirdekCevre.m:
Many networks have a single centre instead of communities: a densely tied core and a periphery tied to the core but sparse within itself. Established researchers among scientists and advanced economies in trade networks are typical cores.

Ağ Masası uses the discrete model of Borgatti and Everett (2000): each node is assigned to the core or the periphery so as to maximise the correlation between the observed network and the ideal pattern (core-core full, periphery-periphery empty). The search uses local improvement from 25 different starts; in tests it reached the brute-force optimum.

A fit above 0.5 indicates a strong core-periphery structure. The block density table shows whether the core really is dense and the periphery really sparse.

aracilar.m:
The most critical nodes of a network are often not those with the most ties but those that join different groups. Ağ Masası shows them in three ways:

  • Betweenness: how many paths pass through the node.
  • Constraint: a low value shows the node joins people who do not know each other (Burt, 1992).
  • Cut point: a node whose removal splits the network; a bridge is a tie that does the same (Hopcroft & Tarjan, 1973).

These nodes carry both opportunity (access to information, influence) and risk (if they leave, the network breaks apart).

kCekirdekY.m:
A k-core is the largest subnetwork in which every member has at least k neighbours inside it. The network is peeled from the outer layer inwards: first nodes of degree 1 are removed, then those of degree 2. A node's core number is the highest k it belongs to (Batagelj & Zaveršnik, 2003).

Unlike the core-periphery model, it splits the network into nested layers rather than two parts. The highest core is the most tightly knit centre of the network.

triadY.m:
In a directed network each pair of nodes is in one of three states: mutual (M), asymmetric (A) or null (N). This is the dyad census.

Each group of three nodes falls into one of 16 types (Batagelj & Mrvar, 2001). The code has three digits and a letter: the numbers of mutual, asymmetric and null pairs, with the letter giving the direction. For example 030T is a transitive hierarchy (A→B, B→C, A→C), 030C a cycle (A→B→C→A) and 300 a fully mutual triple.

Hierarchical networks have many 030T and 021D triads and few cyclic ones; friendship networks stand out with 300 and 201.

kucukDunyaY.m:
Small-world networks are both tightly clustered and short in path length: your neighbours know each other, yet you reach everyone in a few steps (Watts & Strogatz, 1998).

Ağ Masası tests this with σ = (C / Cr) / (L / Lr) (Humphries & Gurney, 2008). C is mean clustering and L mean distance; Cr and Lr are averages over 10 networks rewired at random while keeping the degree distribution (Maslov & Sneppen, 2002). If σ is clearly above 1 the network is a small world. The calculation uses the largest component.

dayaniklilikY.m:
How well does a network withstand the loss of nodes? Ağ Masası removes nodes one by one and plots the share left in the largest part at each step. Three scenarios are compared: an attack starting with the best-connected node (degree is recalculated at each step), an attack starting with the highest betweenness, and random loss (average of 20 orders).

The R index (Schneider et al., 2011) is the area under the curve divided by the number of nodes. If the gap between random loss and targeted attack is large, the network depends on a few key nodes: losing a few distributors in a supply chain, or a few brokers in an organisation, breaks it apart.

qapY.m:
In network data all the ties of one person depend on each other; ordinary statistical tests ignore this dependence and overstate significance. QAP (Krackhardt, 1988) solves this by shuffling the rows and columns of the dependent matrix together, in the same order. Each node's tie pattern is kept, but the link between the node and the predictor is broken. The shuffle is repeated thousands of times and the position of the observed correlation in this distribution gives the p value.

The predictor can be another relation or be derived from an attribute: for a categorical attribute "are they in the same group" (1/0), for a numeric one "how different are the values" (absolute difference).

mrqapY.m:
When several predictors are studied together, MRQAP is used: the dependent relation is estimated as a linear combination of the predictors and the significance of each coefficient is tested by permutation.

Ağ Masası uses double semi-partialling (Dekker et al., 2007): when testing one predictor, it is first cleaned of the others and then its residuals are shuffled. This gives reliable p values even when predictors are correlated.

In the table b is the raw coefficient and β the standardised one; compare the effects of predictors on different scales with β.

pDegeri.m:
In a permutation test, p is the share of random shuffles that gave a value as extreme as the observed one. With 1000 permutations, p = 0.003 means only 3 shuffles gave a value as large as the observed one.

Use p (≥) for a positive expectation, p (≤) for a negative one and the two-sided p if you have no expectation about direction. The number of permutations sets the precision of p: with 1000 permutations values below 0.001 are written as "< 0.001".

Significance says nothing about the size of the effect; report the correlation or the coefficient as well.

cugY.m:
Is a transitivity of 0.13 high or low? A point of comparison is needed. The comparison with random networks in the Tests tab compares your network with hundreds of random networks with the same number of nodes and ties, or with the same degree sequence (Anderson et al., 1999; Maslov & Sneppen, 2002). The table gives the observed value, the random mean, the z score and p values in both directions.

Keeping the degree sequence is the stricter comparison: it shows whether a result comes only from a few highly connected nodes.

dugumTestY.m: Is the in-degree of European countries higher than that of other continents? Are senior staff more central? For such questions use the attribute and position test in the Tests tab. For categorical attributes the F statistic and η² are computed, for numeric attributes Pearson r; the p value comes from shuffling attribute values among the nodes (Borgatti et al., 2018). The classical analysis of variance table should not be used with network data.

asortY.m: The assortativity coefficient shows whether ties form between similar nodes more often than chance (Newman, 2003). +1 means choosing similar others completely, 0 chance, negative values choosing different others. In the Tests tab its significance is tested by permutation. It can be read together with the E-I index in the Groups tab.

modTestY.m: The Louvain method finds communities even in a random network, and modularity comes out above zero. So Q should not be read alone (Guimerà et al., 2004). The significance of community structure test in the Tests tab searches for communities again in random networks with the same degree sequence and compares the observed Q with them.

raporY.m:
The Report tab produces a draft method section from the analyses you ran: the size and type of the network, the measures used, the community and core-periphery analyses, the tests and the drawing method, each with its source. The references are in APA 7 style and were checked against Crossref records.

The Word report contains the network figure, the table of network-level measures, the most central nodes, the community table, the homophily and core-periphery results, small-world, robustness and QAP results if they were run, the method text and the references. Tables and figures are numbered.

The Excel file gives all the measures of every node, the network-level measures, the tie list and the tests on separate sheets.

atifY.m:
If you used Ağ Masası in a study, please cite the software. APA, ISNAD and BibTeX formats are in the "How to cite" window in the File menu, and the method text adds the tool to the references.

Also cite the original sources of the measures and methods; they are given in the method text and on these help pages.

sss.m:
How large can networks be? Networks of up to a few thousand nodes are drawn and measured comfortably. With tens of thousands of nodes, betweenness and closeness can take a long time.

Where are my data stored? Only in this browser (IndexedDB). If you clear the browser data, the project is deleted too, so download the project file.

Why do results differ slightly from Gephi or UCINET? Programs may use different rules for normalisation and for closeness in fragmented networks. Ağ Masası's rules are given in the help and the method text; small differences are normal for random methods such as community detection.

The same person shows up as two nodes. The names are written differently. Fix one in the Data tab so both have the same name, or merge them in the source data.

Can the tool be translated? Yes. Download the translation template from the File menu, translate it and add it with "Load language file".

formul.qap:
xij, yij: cell values between nodes i and j; the diagonal is not used. π: a random ordering of the nodes; rows and columns are shuffled together, so all the ties of a node stay together. R: number of permutations.

In MRQAP bk is the raw and βk the standardised coefficient. The p value uses the double semi-partialling method, shuffling residuals cleaned of the other predictors (Dekker et al., 2007).
formul.cug:
s(G): the measure in the observed network; s(G*): its value in a reference network. s̄ and σs: mean and standard deviation over the reference networks. p (≥) is the share of values at least as high as observed, p (≤) the share at least as low.

T: transitivity. CD: Freeman degree centralisation; di is the degree of a node, n the number of nodes. Reciprocity is the share of mutual ties among all ties.
formul.dugum:
k: number of groups, N: number of valid nodes, ng: nodes in group g. SSB is the between-group, SSW the within-group and SST the total sum of squares. η² shows how much of the difference in position is explained by the groups.

Instead of the classical F table, attribute values are shuffled among nodes R times; Fπ is the value in the shuffled data. For numeric attributes the same is done with Pearson r.
formul.asort:
eij: share of ties with one end in category i and the other in j. ai and bi: shares of tie ends in category i. In an undirected network each tie is counted in both directions.

The expected value is the mean found when attribute values are shuffled among the nodes.
formul.mod:
Aij: 1 if there is a tie between i and j. ki: degree, m: number of ties, δ(ci, cj): 1 if both nodes are in the same community. Q*: the highest modularity found by the Louvain method in a random network with the same degree sequence.

Random networks also show modularity above zero, so Q should be read against random networks, not alone (Guimerà et al., 2004).

testGiris.cug:
To say that a network-level measure is high or low, a point of comparison is needed. This test compares the observed network with many random networks of the same size.

Choose the type of reference networks on the left and run the test.
testGiris.dugum: This test checks whether the position of nodes depends on one of their attributes. Ordinary analysis of variance or correlation gives misleading p values because observations in network data are not independent; here the p value comes from permutations.
testGiris.asort: Assortativity shows whether ties form between similar nodes more often than chance would suggest. It is similar to the E-I index in the Groups tab, but corrects for group sizes and also works with numeric attributes.
testGiris.mod: Community detection methods find communities even in a random network. This test compares the modularity of your network with the modularity found in random networks with the same degree sequence.
